prompt: Under a gate at the end, what happens to how carefully developers check their own work?

choices.text: It stays exactly the same as before the gate
choices.why: The lesson shows Rafael trying four inputs because Lia will try the rest.

choices.text: Developers stop writing code until QA approves the design
choices.why: Nothing in the gate changes when code is written.

choices.text: It drops
choices.why: Right: each person lowers their bar by the height of the next one.

choices.text: It rises, because a tester will catch any mistake and report it to everybody
choices.why: The fear of being caught does not survive a deadline.

prompt: When a defect escapes a team that runs a gate, what does the lesson say the gate turns out to have provided?

choices.text: Proof that the process worked
choices.why: A defect escaped through it.

choices.text: Somebody to blame, since no tester guarantees a release has no defects
choices.why: Right: the promise was never keepable.

choices.text: A guarantee that the defect was minor
choices.why: A gate says nothing about severity.

choices.text: Faster releases
choices.why: The gate is a bottleneck at the end.

prompt: What is "throwing it over the wall"?

choices.text: A tester rejecting a build
choices.why: That is the gate’s side; the wall is the posture that feeds it.

choices.text: Moving a feature to a later sprint because the team ran out of time
choices.why: That is rescheduling, not a hand-off between people.

choices.text: Handing finished work across and forgetting it
choices.why: Right: whatever comes back is treated as a new problem.

choices.text: Releasing to production without any testing at all
choices.why: There may be plenty of testing; the wall is about the hand-off.

prompt: Why is the gate at its weakest exactly when it matters most?

choices.text: Work reaches the tester at the end, so the pressure to approve peaks when there has been least time
choices.why: Right: the bottleneck and the deadline coincide.

choices.text: Testers are tired at the end of the week
choices.why: The cause is structural, not fatigue.

choices.text: Developers refuse to fix defects found by testers they consider adversaries
choices.why: The adversarial tone is real; refusing fixes is not the argument made.

choices.text: Releases happen at night
choices.why: Timing of day is beside the point.

prompt: At Cine Aurora, who decides whether to ship?

choices.text: Lia, because she tested the release
choices.why: She informs the decision; she does not own it.

choices.text: Rafael, who wrote most of the code being released
choices.why: Writing it does not make the release decision his.

choices.text: Célia, who will hear the complaints first at the counter
choices.why: Her view is valuable information; the decision is Joana’s.

choices.text: Joana
choices.why: Right: the product owner, weighing the tester’s information.

prompt: Put the four things Lia gave Joana in the order she gave them.
items: what it costs if it ships
trap: The options come last because they answer the risk the first three describe.

prompt: Which of Lia’s four items is the one testers most often leave out?

choices.text: The cost of shipping
choices.why: Often given, and Lia gave it.

choices.text: A workaround for the defect that the team could apply today
choices.why: Useful, but not the one the lesson singles out.

choices.text: What was not tested
choices.why: Right: it shows the decision-maker where the unknowns are.

choices.text: The defect itself, with its exact reproduction in two commands
choices.why: That is what every report has.

prompt: Kaner defined testing as an investigation that provides stakeholders with what?

choices.text: Information about the quality of the product
choices.why: Right: for somebody else to decide with.

choices.text: Approval to release
choices.why: That is the gate, which the definition avoids.

choices.text: A guarantee that no defects remain in what is about to be released
choices.why: No testing can give that.

choices.text: A count of test cases run
choices.why: Counts are not the point; lesson 22 says why they mislead.

prompt: Lia believes a defect should hold the release. Which sentence fits this lesson best?

choices.text: "QA has failed this build."
choices.why: A verdict with nothing to weigh.

choices.text: Nothing: a tester must stay neutral and only list defects
choices.why: Giving information is not being neutral; a view is welcome.

choices.text: "This cannot ship."
choices.why: A standoff, inviting the question of who outranks whom.

choices.text: "I would not ship this: every Sunday morning customer pays too much."
choices.why: Right: a plain recommendation with the evidence behind it.

prompt: Match each of Bolton’s three stories to what it tells.
hint: Product, testing, quality of the testing.

pairs.right: how you looked, and how well

prompt: Whose book gave the whole-team approach its name?

choices.text: W. Edwards Deming
choices.why: Deming argued about process in manufacturing.

choices.text: Lisa Crispin and Janet Gregory
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Cem Kaner
choices.why: Kaner’s is the definition of testing as information.

choices.text: Michael Bolton, who wrote about the three stories a report tells
choices.why: Bolton’s is the three stories.

prompt: In Lia’s third week, what was most of the value she created?
hint: Count the hours spent checking finished work.

choices.text: Checking finished features
choices.why: A minority of the week.

choices.text: Writing automated tests for every feature
choices.why: Rafael writes the tests in the pairing session; Lia suggests inputs.

choices.text: Work done before or while code was written, and teaching others to see problems
choices.why: Right: that is what makes a tester a multiplier.

choices.text: Approving the release on Thursday
choices.why: She wrote information for Joana; she approved nothing.

prompt: What does "tester as a coach" mean in this lesson?

choices.text: Making the tester unnecessary within a year
choices.why: The goal is to point their attention at harder problems.

choices.text: Their testing knowledge spreads through the team
choices.why: Right: developers asking about sixty exactly without being prompted.

choices.text: A tester who no longer tests
choices.why: The lesson says that is the misunderstanding.

choices.text: A tester who manages the developers and assigns their work every morning
choices.why: Coaching is not managing.

prompt: Which risk is not the product owner’s alone to accept, by this lesson?

choices.text: A typo on the help page
choices.why: A team can choose to ship a typo.

choices.text: Shipping a feature a week later
choices.why: A commercial trade-off: hers.

choices.text: A slow seat map on old phones
choices.why: Commercial, and hers to weigh.

choices.text: Charging people over sixty full price, against the statute
choices.why: Right: a team cannot choose to break a statute.

prompt: What separates a tester’s view from a veto, by the lesson’s four steps?

choices.text: Including a reproduction
choices.why: Step two; evidence supports either.

choices.text: Copying the report to the whole company
choices.why: Not one of the steps, and not how disagreement works.

choices.text: Saying what would change your mind
choices.why: Right: it hands the decision-maker a way forward.

choices.text: Stating the recommendation in the first sentence of the report, in bold
choices.why: Step one; a veto also comes first.

prompt: Joana ships against Lia’s recommendation. What does the lesson say Lia should do first?

choices.text: Refuse to test the next release
choices.why: That is a gate by other means.

choices.text: Record what was known, recommended and decided
choices.why: Right: then help reduce the accepted risk.

choices.text: Escalate to the company’s directors
choices.why: Escalation is for risks beyond the team, like the law.

choices.text: Keep a list of decisions that went wrong, to show later
choices.why: That is keeping score.

prompt: A developer, unsure whether a change works, says "I’ll send it to QA and see". What does that tell you about the team, by the lesson’s test?

choices.text: The whole-team approach is working
choices.why: It is the opposite sign.

choices.text: The tester is working as a gate, whatever the job title says
choices.why: Right: the other answer is "ask Lia what she would try".

choices.text: The team trusts its tester
choices.why: It relies on them as a gate, which is different.

choices.text: The developer is careless
choices.why: The arrangement produces the habit.
